title: Corrective IR for Live Venues
description: A live six-channel hybrid system combining per-channel corrective FIRs for the initial response with a separately applied target-hall reverberation tail.
question: Can corrective IR make one venue sound like another?
body: Playing a target hall’s impulse response (IR) in another venue also adds the current venue’s response. I wanted to correct the current room’s coloration before adding the target hall’s reverberation.

I measured six surround-loudspeaker-to-microphone paths and used Python to align them with the target IR. I created a corrective FIR filter for each channel, focusing on the first 40 ms and the 125 Hz–4 kHz band. The filters use regularization to limit excessive gain.

Max/MSP applies a separate corrective filter to each of the six surround speakers in real time. Convology XT adds the target hall’s reverberation from about 200 ms onward. The main PA carries the direct sound.

At the fourth-row center, mean spectral error fell from 2.69 to 2.24 dB across six channels. This comparison uses the same path measurements that were used to create the filters. It does not establish improvement at other seats or a perceptual match to the target hall.

title: Live Immersive Audio Processor Studies
description: Measuring how Sound xR Image and L-ISA turn sound position and width into loudspeaker outputs, then testing models against new speaker layouts.
question: What changes at the speakers when we move a sound?
body: This study began after using Sound xR Image for an outdoor performance. I wanted to connect the controls on screen with what each speaker actually receives. The photos below show the Sound xR work that started the project.

I extended the investigation to L-ISA with digital loopback measurements. Both studies compare measured outputs with mathematical models; they describe the tested software and settings. Listening tests and measurements across audience seats remain future work.

summary.en: Measured Sound xR Image and L-ISA to understand how position and width affect speaker outputs. Tested the models on new layouts.
summary.ko: Sound xR Image와 L-ISA에서 위치와 폭에 따른 스피커 출력 변화를 측정하고, 새로운 배치에서 모델을 검증했습니다.

problem.en: I wanted to understand how position and width controls change the signals sent to speakers.
problem.ko: 위치와 폭 조절이 각 스피커로 보내는 신호를 어떻게 바꾸는지 알고 싶었습니다.

design.en: Measured Sound xR output levels with DME7 and Smaart, and L-ISA level, frequency response, and delay with digital loopback sweeps.
design.ko: DME7과 Smaart로 Sound xR의 출력 레벨을, 디지털 루프백 스윕으로 L-ISA의 레벨·주파수 응답·지연을 측정했습니다.

analysis.en: Compared candidate models, tested predictions on new layouts, and used controlled changes to investigate failures.

title: Multichannel Live Mixing
description: Exploring immersive sound image control and spatial mixing approaches for small performance venues.
question: Can sound placement match what audiences see?
body: I tested whether speaker placement and console routing could align the perceived direction of sound with what the audience sees on stage.
I built a 3.1 system with additional rear-stage speakers. Vocals, kick, snare, and bass went to the center; other instruments and reverberation were spread across the left, right, and rear speakers.

The sources were clearly separated, but informal audience feedback suggested they sounded disconnected. This led me to consider how listeners combine sounds into one scene. A structured listening test is still needed.

summary.en: Built a 3.1 system with rear speakers. Informal feedback suggested the sound felt too separated.
summary.ko: 3.1채널과 후방 스피커를 구성했습니다. 관객 반응에서 소리가 서로 떨어져 들리는 한계를 발견했습니다.

title: Real-Time Remote Multichannel Audio
description: Exploring real-time networked audio systems for remote musical interaction and collaboration.
question: Can musicians collaborate across distance?
body: I tested real-time multichannel audio transmission between two remote DAWs for recording, mixing, and performance.

I explored commercial network-audio approaches and tested relay and peer-to-peer tools, including ffmpeg, JACK Audio, and JackTrip. Audio could be sent, but playback did not remain sample-accurate over time.

The tests pointed to clock drift between the two systems as a key limitation. Over time, this was associated with buffer errors and audible clicks. Synchronization and adaptive resampling are next steps to investigate.

summary.en: Tested audio between remote DAWs. Clock drift limited stable playback over time.
summary.ko: 떨어진 DAW 사이의 오디오 전송을 시험했습니다. 시간이 지나며 쌓이는 클락 차이가 안정적인 재생을 제한했습니다.

title: Performer-Tailored Electronic Drum Module
description: A Max/MSP drum module with velocity zones and sample layers shaped around an individual performer’s dynamic range.
question: Can electronic drums adapt to each player’s touch?
body: The fixed response of a commercial electronic drum module may not match how a particular drummer plays. I built a Max/MSP module to adjust sample choice and playback level to one player’s striking range.

The patch routes MIDI notes to drum sounds and uses custom velocity ranges for snare and ride samples. MIDI velocity sets playback level, CC4 controls hi-hat openness, and the player can set gain, pan, and output for each drum.
The mapping is adjusted manually for one player. It does not learn automatically. Recorded velocity distributions and a controlled comparison with a fixed mapping are still needed.

summary.en: Built a Max/MSP drum module with manually adjusted velocity ranges for one player.
summary.ko: 한 연주자의 타격 범위에 맞춰 소리 반응을 수동으로 조절하는 Max/MSP 드럼 모듈을 만들었습니다.

problem.en: I wanted the electronic drum module’s response to match one player’s dynamics more closely.
problem.ko: 전자드럼의 소리 반응을 한 연주자의 연주 다이나믹에 맞추고 싶었습니다.

design.en: I built a Max/MSP module with adjustable snare and ride sample ranges, hi-hat control, and separate mixing settings for each drum.
design.ko: 스네어·라이드 샘플 선택 구간과 하이햇 반응, 드럼별 믹싱을 조절하는 Max/MSP 모듈을 만들었습니다.

analysis.en: I adjusted the mapping manually for one player. Velocity distributions and a before/after comparison are still needed.
analysis.ko: 한 연주자에 맞춰 소리 반응을 수동으로 조절했습니다. 타격 세기 분포와 조절 전후 비교는 추후 확인해야 합니다.

title: Trackform — Audio-to-MIDI & ML Evaluation
description: An audio-to-MIDI workspace exploring model adaptation, held-out evaluation, and the gap between rendered music and real recordings.
question: Can AI ease live preparation while preserving the artist’s musical expression?
body: Trackform turns recorded music into editable MIDI for performance preparation. It combines specialist transcription models, Demucs stem separation, a piano-roll editor, audition, and MIDI export. The Next.js interface and FastAPI processing pipeline also support a local Tauri desktop application.

The ML question is whether adapting a pretrained model to the actual processing path improves transcription on unfamiliar recordings. Piano uses Transkun, bass uses Basic Pitch with hybrid post-processing, and drums use ADTOF on HT-Demucs stems. These are existing models integrated into an assistive editing workflow; generated notes remain open to correction.

ADTOF fine-tuning targeted separation artifacts and weak drum classes. Slakh supplies paired rendered audio and MIDI labels, making supervised adaptation to separated stems possible. The reduced experiment used 40 Slakh train songs for training and a separate 16 for validation. MDB Drums, 23 real recordings, was reserved for test evaluation. The original plan included real-recording training and rehearsal data; ADTOF data required access approval and the ENST download was too slow, so those conditions were not run.

The experiment compared pretrained weights (A0), full fine-tuning (A1), and a frozen convolutional/batch-normalization block with trainable GRU and output layers (A4f). The initial learning rate was 1e-4, one fifth of the original setting. A smaller update and frozen feature extractor were conservative adaptation choices, not a demonstrated optimum from a learning-rate sweep. The implementation uses Adam, binary cross-entropy, seed 0, validation-loss early stopping (patience 3), and learning-rate reduction. Candidate selection then uses validation F1.

A4f led rendered validation: F1 rose from 0.695 to 0.786. On MDB, it fell from 0.859 to 0.816; the paired difference was −0.043 with a 95% bootstrap interval of [−0.066, −0.022]. Hi-hat and tom performance declined despite gains for kick and cymbal. The candidate was rejected and pretrained ADTOF remained the default. A1 also scored 0.816 on MDB, but that additional test was recorded outside the planned single-candidate selection rule.

This reversal is consistent with domain shift and loss of useful pretrained behavior, but it does not isolate the cause. A proposed follow-up would compare rendered-only training, real-recording training, and mixed training with rehearsal, each with frozen and unfrozen feature blocks. Data access, matched training budgets, multiple seeds, real-recording validation, and a fresh untouched final test set would be needed. Per-class errors and paired intervals would determine adoption; repeated inspection of MDB should not become test-set tuning.

This is AI-assisted development with documented model integration, fine-tuning code, and evaluation records. The research contribution presented here is the question, experimental comparison, and evidence-based adoption decision. The project does not claim a new foundation model or proven workflow benefit. MIDI correction effort and rehearsal preparation time still require user evaluation.

title: CI Interactive Ensemble Room
description: A Korean-language interactive listening prototype for CI users, with sound setup, stem mixing, cue comparisons, and personal reports. Uses pink-noise placeholders; user evaluation is still planned.
question: Can listeners discover their own musical cues—and find them again in a song?
body: What should listeners be able to choose for themselves? Building sound systems for venues and a drum response for one performer led to a Korean-language interactive listening prototype for cochlear implant (CI) users: CI Interactive Ensemble Room. The project has moved from design documents to a clickable browser prototype.

The implemented flow runs from sound activation through six sound-setup steps, an ensemble room, cue questions, reflection, and a personal listening report. Setup covers listening equipment and connection, comfortable volume, left–right balance, tone, instrument levels, and optional bass support. Listeners can revisit these choices from the ensemble room.

In the ensemble room, listeners can solo or mute cajon, double bass, and trumpet, change their levels, loop a section, or alternate between sounds. Optional lanes, waveforms, spectra, and performer animations follow audio timing. A listen-first sequence moves from sound alone to visual guidance and back to listening.

Two cue-question sets use comparisons and reflections without correct answers or scores. The report describes patterns in the current session and lets listeners revise their own explanations. Settings, interaction logs, and responses are stored in the browser; JSON and CSV export and full data deletion are implemented. The prototype uses React, TypeScript, Web Audio, and Canvas 2D.

The audio is still a placeholder: each instrument uses independent pink noise, with no real recordings or pitched melody. The first song structure follows Happy Birthday to You; the second song is undecided. The pitch comparison substitutes a change of noise frequency band, so it cannot yet test musical pitch perception. The interface and audio controls are implemented, but music-listening benefits remain untested.

The repository records browser checks on 23 October 2026 for the main flow, audio-node levels, mobile and desktop layouts, and automated accessibility checks. These are implementation checks, not results from CI participants. Next steps are selecting the second song, recording stems and comparison clips, checking real-device playback and latency including Bluetooth and CI streaming, and conducting initial usability sessions with 2–5 CI users. Longer-term learning and transfer to unfamiliar music require a separate study.

galleryCaptions.ko: 합주실 — 카혼·콘트라베이스·트럼펫을 혼자 듣거나 함께 듣고, 구간과 반복을 고릅니다. 실제 프로토타입 화면이며 소리는 핑크노이즈 자리표시입니다.
galleryCaptions.en: Ensemble room — solo or combine cajon, double bass, and trumpet, then choose a section or loop. Captured from the working prototype; audio uses pink-noise placeholders.

galleryCaptions.ko: 악기별 믹싱 — 악기 크기와 프리셋, 저음 도움을 조절하는 패널입니다. 기본 설정 상태를 캡처했습니다.
galleryCaptions.en: Stem mixing — instrument levels, presets, and bass support in the expanded controls, captured at their default settings.

galleryCaptions.ko: 단서 비교 — 두 소리를 듣고 차이와 느낀 단서를 표시합니다. 참여자의 응답이 아닌, 응답 전 연습 화면입니다.
galleryCaptions.en: Cue comparison — listen to two sounds and describe their differences. This is the unanswered practice screen, not a participant result.
